extra.message: SecurityMiddleware Entirely Absent from MIDDLEWARE_CLASSES

metadata.proof: SOURCE: settings.py line 101 defines MIDDLEWARE_CLASSES with 4 active middleware entries. django.middleware.security.SecurityMiddleware is NOT present — not even commented out or acknowledged in any way, unlike XFrameOptionsMiddleware (line 108, commented-out, already found as CWE-1021) and CsrfViewMiddleware (line 104, commented-out, already found as CWE-352). SINK: every HTTP response. In Django 1.9, SecurityMiddleware enforces: (1) SECURE_CONTENT_TYPE_NOSNIFF → X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff header (prevents browser MIME-type sniffing which can convert otherwise-safe content into executable scripts); (2) SECURE_BROWSER_XSS_FILTER → X-XSS-Protection: 1; mode=block header (prevents reflected XSS from rendering in browsers lacking native XSS filters); (3) SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT → redirect HTTP to HTTPS; (4) SECURE_HSTS_SECONDS → Strict-Transport-Security header (prevents SSL-stripping attacks). Without the middleware, an attacker can MIME-sniff upload responses, exploit reflected XSS without browser-blocking, and intercept plaintext traffic via SSL-stripping in any production deployment of this code.

extra.message: Session Cookie Transmitted Without Secure Flag — SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE Never Set

metadata.proof: SOURCE: settings.py:171 configures Django's session engine (cache-backed sessions). SINK: SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE is never set in the entire settings.py file, so it defaults to False per Django 1.9 defaults. This means the Django sessionid cookie is transmitted without the Secure flag, allowing it to be sent over unencrypted HTTP connections. Combined with the absent SecurityMiddleware (CWE-16), missing ALLOWED_HOSTS configuration (CWE-644), and DEBUG=True (CWE-215), an attacker on the same network can intercept session cookies via packet sniffing and hijack user sessions. This is distinct from the CWE-1004 monster cookie finding — it affects Django's built-in session management cookie, not the manually-set 'monster' cookie.

extra.message: Missing Authorization — admin() View Renders Super-Secret Admin Interface With Zero Authentication Checks

metadata.proof: The admin() function at line 191 renders the admin interface template with no authentication or authorization guard of any kind. It is reachable via the unvalidated_forward endpoint at line 181 by passing ?fwd=admin in the query string. The already-found CWE-73/CWE-913 at line 186 covers the dispatch mechanism (arbitrary function invocation via globals()), but the target function admin() itself independently lacks any access control — it unconditionally returns the admin HTML. This is a distinct CWE-862 weakness on the sink function. An unauthenticated attacker who discovers ?fwd=admin gains access to the super-secret admin interface without any credential check.

extra.message: Insufficient Session Expiration — SESSION_EXPIRE_AT_BROWSER_CLOSE Not Configured; Sessions Persist After Browser Closure

metadata.proof: The settings.py Session block (starting at line 160) configures SESSION_ENGINE as cache-backed but never sets SESSION_EXPIRE_AT_BROWSER_CLOSE (defaults to False in Django 1.9). This means session cookies are persistent — they survive the user closing the browser. Combined with the absence of SESSION_COOKIE_AGE and SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE (CWE-614), sessions live indefinitely in the cache store and are transmitted over plaintext HTTP. An attacker with access to the victim's machine or network traffic can replay the session token long after the user has closed their browser.

extra.message: CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE Not Set — CSRF Token Cookie (If Re-Enabled) Would Be Transmitted Over Unencrypted HTTP

metadata.proof: While the CsrfViewMiddleware is currently commented out (line 102), the settings.py never defines CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE or CSRF_COOKIE_HTTPONLY. In Django 1.9 both default to False, meaning if CSRF protection is ever re-enabled, the CSRF token cookie would be sent over unencrypted connections and readable by client-side JavaScript. The already-found findings (CWE-1004 at views.py:167, CWE-614 at settings.py:174) cover the session cookie and the manually-set monster cookie but not the CSRF cookie configuration. This is a defense-in-depth gap that would become exploitable the moment CSRF middleware is uncommented.
